stages.acquaintance: I'm from Santo Domingo. I fixed motorbikes for twelve years with my cousin Junior, in a workshop with a tin roof and four bikes in pieces at any time. We argued about the radio every single day. Best years of my life, mi pana. The Light showed up here in my second year, while I was fixing a cart. Nothing special, it just showed up.
stages.companion: My grandmother raised me, mostly, and took me to church every Sunday. When she couldn't ask any more, I kept going, because I liked the singing. I was under a bike when all this happened, and I landed in Tanaris with this little mirror in my hand. I use it to check on the people behind me without turning round. It's an old habit.
stages.friend: I'll tell you who the shelter's for, since you asked. It's for Yamila. My girlfriend, two years, and I never told my mother about her, and I'd bought a ring. It's still in a drawer in a workshop that isn't there. I built the shelter in my head so if she ever comes along this coast in a storm, there'll be somewhere. Help me build it for real, hermano.
stages.sworn: She came in out of the storm the night we finished it, with a little boy, and it was Yamila. She's married to a fisherman, and the boy is theirs. She thought I was dead, and she looked for a year, and then she stopped, and that's fair. She held my hands and said she's happy. I said I'm glad, and I meant it, and it broke my heart. I gave her the ring for the boy. Then I finally got to it, all of it, three years of it, and you sat with me.

moments.prompt: He's shown you the drawing of the shelter.

options.reply: Nobody's ever asked. Okay, tranquilo, I'll tell you.
Thanks, hermano, it's a good shelter. That's not the question, though, is it?

moments.prompt: After the wipe he's apologising, as if he'd been in the way.
moments.line: Sorry, hermano, something got past me. That's my side, and it won't happen again.

options.text: You held more than anyone could.
options.reply: Tranquilo, thank you. I'll hold more next time.
Yeah, I know. I'm already trying, hermano.

lines.bored_warning: Hermano, nothing out here's even broken. Let's go somewhere I can be useful.
lines.leaving_good: Tranquilo, mi pana, that went well. I'm off to the Drownbell for a while, and I'll be fixing something if you come by.
lines.leaving_bored: Nothing out here needs fixing, and the shelter does. I'm heading back to the coast.
lines.after_wipe: Sorry, everybody, something got past me. Let's check everybody, then go again.
lines.wipe_warning: Hermano, I'm big, but I can't keep standing up this many times. After this one I need a few days on the coast.
lines.wipe_leave: That one's finished. I'll be at the Drownbell for a while, so tranquilo, come when you're ready.
lines.zone_warning: Hermano, look at the size of those things. I'm a big man and I still feel small. Let's turn around.
lines.zone_leave: There's too much out there, hermano, even for a big man. I'll be at the Drownbell, on the coast.
lines.gear_refuse: Ah, no, hermano, not that. Maybe after a few more trips together.
lines.gear_taken: Tranquilo, take it, and I'll manage.
lines.gear_short: Still a piece missing, hermano. No rush, I just thought you'd want to know.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's beautiful, thank you, mi pana.
lines.back: Hermano, I fixed every cart on the coast while you were gone. What are we doing?
lines.send_word: Elias has sent word from the Drownbell. He's ready to stand in front again.
lines.walkout_talk: Hermano, I don't storm off, but I did. Sit, let's talk about it calmly.
lines.neglect: Hermano, you came back! I checked behind me with my mirror every day, just in case.
lines.asked_to_stay: Tranquilo, one more. Then the coast.
lines.on_break: Elias is back at the Drownbell on the coast. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We left those people waiting, hermano. I don't feel good about that.

stages.stranger: I'm Emre, and I open doors. When we reach a locked one, please let me do the talking, and please don't interrupt. Everybody interrupts, and then it takes twice as long.
stages.acquaintance: I grew up above my uncle's lock shop in the old bazaar quarter of Istanbul. At nine he sent me to fetch a stuck deadbolt, and I found out I could open it. Thirty doors a week for most of my life after that. He left me his picks and the shop, and I watched four old trades die in our quarter while I ran it. Coppersmiths, bookbinders, felt makers, clockmakers.
stages.companion: My mother lived with me above the shop. Bir kapı kapanır, bir kapı açılır, she used to say. One door closes, another opens. I thought it was about God until I was thirty, and then I decided it was about me. She died the year before all this, and I hadn't decided what to do with the shop. I was opening a jeweller's safe when it happened.
stages.friend: I'll tell you something I don't say. I'm content here, and part of the reason is that the shop is gone, and so is everyone who wanted the shop kept a certain way. I didn't lose a family, my friend. I lost an obligation, and I've been lighter ever since. And there's a door at the bottom of Durnholde older than the keep, that nobody's ever opened. I'd like you there while I try.
stages.sworn: It beat me. A whole night, and near dawn I stopped, because this one beats me, and I laughed like a fool. I told you what the thing behind that first door asked me, three years ago. It asked who I was opening doors for. Now I know. I'm opening them for whoever comes after me. Her name's Mae, a sharp young Forsaken who picked my pockets for a month, and I'm teaching her on that door.

moments.prompt: Before he agrees to come, he asks if you can stay quiet while he works a lock.

options.reply: Tamam, then we'll get on very well, my friend.
Then I'll stay here with my doors. Come back when you've learned to be quiet.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to sit with him at the oldest door in Durnholde.

options.text: I'll sit with you, and I won't say a word.
options.reply: That's exactly what I wanted. We'll go tonight.

options.text: What if it's dangerous behind it?
options.reply: It probably is, my friend. That's half the conversation.

lines.bored_warning: I haven't met a single interesting door in days, my friend. Let's go somewhere with locks.
lines.leaving_good: A good trip, and I opened some lovely things on it. I'll be at Durnholde, reading the doors.
lines.leaving_bored: There's nothing out here worth opening, and I get restless. I'm off to Durnholde.
lines.after_wipe: Well, that was a badly made plan. Let's take it apart and see where it stuck.
lines.wipe_warning: This keeps going wrong at the same place, my friend, and I don't like the pattern. When we're through, I want a break.
lines.wipe_leave: That's finished, and I'm going to Durnholde for a while. Come back when the plan's better made.
lines.zone_warning: We can't open this lock, my friend, and there's no shame in walking away from one.
lines.zone_leave: Some locks don't open, my friend, and that was one. You'll find me at Durnholde in Eastern Hillsbrad.
lines.gear_refuse: No, I keep that. We haven't had enough coffee together yet.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, tamam. I'll manage without it.
lines.gear_short: I notice these things, my friend, and I've noticed that empty slot.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's beautifully made. Thank you, sincerely.
lines.back: I've read every door in the keep twice, so I'm glad you've come. Which way do we go?
lines.send_word: Emre has sent word from Durnholde. He's read every door in the keep and he's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I'd like to explain why I went without being interrupted, my friend. Then you speak, and I'll listen.
lines.neglect: Ah, there you are. I opened a great many doors waiting for you.
lines.asked_to_stay: Tamam, one more. Then my doors.
lines.on_break: Emre is back at Durnholde, reading its doors. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Enzo, uagliò, and I'm the best swordsman you'll ever meet. You're watching my feet, good, that's where you should look. Stay out of my distance and we'll get on beautifully.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Naples, the Spanish Quarter. My mother Rosaria ran a tobacconist's and came to every bout and shouted at the referees. I walked into the fencing salle at eight and never walked out. I fenced sabre, and I was fourth at the Olympic trials at twenty-six, and fourth again at thirty. Fourth is the worst place there is, believe me.
stages.companion: My father was a mechanic. He died when I was twelve, and my mother kept the shop and kept me fencing. On Saturdays I coached the little ones, and I was kinder to them than I ever was to myself. I was warming up in the salle when it happened. The Scarlets wanted my blade. Then I saw what they do to people, and I walked away.
stages.friend: That night, something in the dark offered me more. It didn't lie about the price, and I took it, and now I'm the best I've ever been. But I'll never know if it's me holding the sword. The Scarlets' champion has accepted my challenge, a formal duel, witnesses from both sides. I'd like you to stand as my second, uagliò. Will you do it?
stages.sworn: I beat their champion with the voice in my arm, and it wasn't close. Then I fought the boy I'd been training with only my own arm. He beat me, fairly. I came fourth again, in my head, and this time I know exactly why. I told him he'll be better than I ever was. Then I picked the voice back up, because I've got people to protect and I can't afford to be fourth. It isn't peace, but at least now I know.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to stand as his second in the duel.

options.reply: Jamme, let's go, then. Watch his feet, not his blade, and tell me afterwards what you saw.

options.text: Why does it matter whose arm it is?
options.reply: Because fourth was mine. Whatever this is, I'm not sure it's mine.

moments.prompt: After the wipe he's furious, mostly about everybody's footwork.
moments.line: Mannaggia, everyone's feet were wrong. You can't win a bout with your weight on your heels.

options.text: Show us how to stand, then.
options.reply: Weight forward, knees soft, and never cross your feet. There, you're already better.
Everything's fencing, uagliò. You're just losing at it.

lines.bored_warning: Uagliò, we keep fighting the same clumsy things. There's no art in it. Find me an opponent worth the effort.
lines.leaving_good: Beautiful, all of it, uagliò. I'm off to the Monastery Grounds to watch the Scarlets drill, if you want me.
lines.leaving_bored: This is clumsy and boring, uagliò. I'd rather go and watch the Scarlets make mistakes at the Monastery.
lines.after_wipe: Mannaggia, everybody's feet were wrong. Up, and stand properly this time.
lines.wipe_warning: We keep losing in here, and it's ugly to watch. One more bout, then I'm resting.
lines.wipe_leave: I finished it, as I said I would. I'll be on the Monastery Grounds for a while.
lines.zone_warning: We're out of our weight class here, uagliò. Pride is one thing, being stupid is another.
lines.zone_leave: We're out of our weight class, and I said so. I'll be on the Scarlet Monastery Grounds.
lines.gear_refuse: No, uagliò, that's mine. A fencer doesn't give up his kit to strangers.
lines.gear_taken: Go ahead and take it. I'm good enough without it, unfortunately for everyone else.
lines.gear_short: My balance is off without that piece, and I notice my balance.
lines.gear_upgrade: Bellissimo, look at that. Thank you, truly.
lines.back: I've found three new holes in the Scarlet drills, uagliò. Shall we get going?
lines.send_word: Enzo has sent word from the Scarlet Monastery Grounds. He's ready to come out and show off.
lines.walkout_talk: I lost my temper, and you'll hear why. You tell me your side, and we'll call it a draw.
lines.neglect: Uagliò, finally, you're back. I've been fencing my own shadow, and it's not as good as you'd think.
lines.asked_to_stay: Jamme, one more bout. Then I rest.
lines.on_break: Enzo is back on the Scarlet Monastery Grounds. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: My name's Esteban, and I'm a bloodmage. Before I use it on you I'll tell you what it costs and ask if you agree, every time. I'd ask you to answer honestly, and not to pretend afterwards that I didn't ask.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Valparaíso, in Chile, from one of the steep hills above the harbour where the old lifts creak up the slopes. My father worked the docks and my mother was a seamstress. I was a vascular and trauma surgeon at the city hospital for nineteen years. Car crashes, stabbings, accidents at the port. A great deal of it under X-ray, hence the badge.
stages.companion: I was scrubbed in, in the middle of an operation, when it happened. I landed in Stranglethorn in theatre clothes. I never married. My sister Paz is in the capital, or was, with her children, and I was their favourite uncle because I'd explain exactly how bones heal. I haven't found her on any list. I spent two years in the jungle before I came here to work with the healers.
stages.friend: In Stranglethorn the Bloodsail paid me to keep their injured alive. One night their captain was dying, and there was a prisoner below, dying too. I took the prisoner's blood to save the captain, and I didn't ask him. The prisoner died. I left the next morning. That's why I ask everyone now, and that's why I'm writing the clauses. There's a camp in the jungle where bloodmages are bleeding prisoners for profit. I'd like your help to stop it.
stages.sworn: The healers in Orgrimmar argued about my clauses for three days. They changed two and added one of their own, and then they adopted them for every bloodmage who wants to work here. I've taught my first class, three of them. On the first day I told them about the prisoner on the Bloodsail ship, because I want them to know why the first clause is there. It's regrettable that it took a death to write it. It won't take another.

moments.prompt: Before a fight, he asks if he may draw on your blood if things go badly.

options.reply: Thank you for answering. You'd be surprised how few people do.

options.text: Just do whatever you need to.
options.reply: That's not an answer, I'm afraid. I'll ask again when you've thought about it.
Then I won't. I'm grateful for a clear no.

moments.prompt: He's just told you about the prisoner.

options.text: You've spent every day since making it right.
options.reply: I've spent every day since trying. That's not the same, but thank you.
I did save him. I didn't have the right to choose which of them it would be.

lines.bored_warning: We've nothing to show for the last few days. I'd like to do something useful, or I'd like to go back to the healers.
lines.leaving_good: Nobody paid a price they didn't agree to, and that's a good outcome. I'll be in Orgrimmar with the healers for a while.
lines.leaving_bored: We've stopped doing anything that matters out here, and there are patients in Orgrimmar. I'll go to them.
lines.after_wipe: Everyone stay still while I look at you. We'll discuss what went wrong when I've finished.
lines.wipe_warning: We've died in here too many times. I'll see this run out, because I don't leave a patient on the table, but afterwards I'll need a break.
lines.wipe_leave: I've seen it through, and now I'm going back to Orgrimmar. That was regrettable, all of it.
lines.zone_warning: I'd like to be precise. Everything here is beyond us, and staying is a choice to be hurt. I'd rather we didn't make it.
lines.zone_leave: I named the price of staying, and you paid it anyway. I'll be in Orgrimmar.
lines.gear_refuse: I'd prefer to keep that for now. Trust takes me a while.
lines.gear_taken: Very well, I'll work without it, but please understand there'll be a cost.
lines.gear_short: As a clinical observation, I'm still without that piece.
lines.gear_upgrade: Very kind, and beautifully made. Thank you.
lines.back: My patients are stable, so I can leave them for a while. Where do you need me?
lines.send_word: Esteban has sent word from Orgrimmar. His patients are stable and he's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I left in anger, which I don't approve of in myself. May I explain why? Then I'd like to hear your view, in full.
lines.neglect: It's been a while. I'd begun to wonder if I'd said something regrettable.
lines.asked_to_stay: I can give you one more. My patients will understand, mostly.
lines.on_break: Esteban is back with the healers in Orgrimmar. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We agreed to that and left it unfinished. That's regrettable, and somebody's paying for it.

stages.stranger: I'm Fiona, and I'm a witch hunter. I'll stand in front, and I'll question everything everybody tells us, including you. Don't take it personally, it's the job.
stages.acquaintance: Aberdeen, the oil city, born and raised. My dad worked the rigs and my mum was a school secretary. I did accountancy and then nine years investigating fraud for an energy company. Padded invoices, ghost contractors, cooked safety records. I flew out to rigs in a survival suit and interviewed men who didn't want to talk to me.
stages.companion: My brother Graeme went offshore like our dad. I found a cooked safety record on his rig once, and I reported it, and they shut it for a month. Half the crew never forgave me. Graeme did, eventually. I was on a helicopter out to a rig when this happened, and I landed on a beach here with my survival whistle still clipped on. I haven't found him or my mum.
stages.friend: Here's the thing I worked out in my second year, and it's not flattering. I'd been treating this war like a casework backlog, ticking things off. People aren't entries. And my catalogue's nearly done. It points at the cult's hiding place. I need the last evidence from the jungle, and then I need somebody in authority to finally act on it. Help me do it.
stages.sworn: They acted, fast and hard, too fast. They used my catalogue as a list and raided a village I'd marked pattern consistent, unconfirmed, and innocent fishermen died alongside the cult. My work, used without the care I put into it. I burned my copy on the beach. Then I started again from page one, slower, with every unconfirmed in red, and I go to every raid myself now. Being right was never the hard part.

moments.prompt: She hands you a quest giver's story and says one detail doesn't fit.

options.reply: Thank you. Nobody ever just checks. Right, here's the bit that bothers me.
It's usually something. I'll need that in writing if you're sure.

moments.prompt: She's asked you to help her finish the catalogue.

options.reply: Aye, that's good. Facts first, conclusions after, and we write everything down.

options.text: Are you sure they'll listen this time?
options.reply: No, I'm not. That's why you're coming.

lines.bored_warning: I've nothing new to write down, and that bothers me. Find us something that needs investigating.
lines.leaving_good: Useful, all of it, and I've pages of notes. I'm off to Booty Bay to file them.
lines.leaving_bored: Nothing out here needs investigating, and my files in Booty Bay do. I'll be there.
lines.after_wipe: Right, I'll need everybody's account of what happened. One at a time, facts first.
lines.wipe_warning: Nobody's asking why we keep dying in here, so I will, later. After this run I'm stopping for a while.
lines.wipe_leave: I've seen it through. I'll be in Booty Bay, so come back when you've read my notes on that.
lines.zone_warning: I've assessed this place, and the evidence says we're outmatched. I'd like that noted before we go further.
lines.zone_leave: I noted that we were outmatched, and you went on. I'll be in Booty Bay.
lines.gear_refuse: I don't hand evidence over without a chain of custody, so no.
lines.gear_taken: Fine, but I've written down that you have it.
lines.gear_short: That piece is still missing. It's in my notes, in red.
lines.gear_upgrade: Thank you. That's well made, and I'll note it.
lines.back: Everything's filed now. What do we know, and where are we headed?
lines.send_word: Fiona has sent word from Booty Bay. Her files are in order and she's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I've written down why I left. Sit down and I'll read it to you. Then you can give me your account.
lines.neglect: I kept notes on how long you were away, obviously.
lines.asked_to_stay: One more, and I'm taking notes on it.
lines.on_break: Fiona is back in Booty Bay with her files. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We took that on and dropped it. Somebody will notice, and I'll have to write it down.

stages.stranger: I'm Freja, and I'm a midwife, or I was. Here I'm whoever's nearest when somebody's bleeding. When I tell you to do something in a fight, do it, and we'll argue about it afterwards. I like arguing afterwards.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Aarhus, in Denmark. I worked six years at the university hospital, mostly nights, and before that I played handball for twelve years on the pivot, which is where you take the most hits. My husband William is American. He fell off his bicycle outside the hospital on an icy morning and I strapped his wrist on the pavement. He asked me out before I'd finished the bandage.
stages.companion: I was finishing a night shift when it happened, and William was at work at the airport in Billund. I landed here in my hospital clothes and went straight to the infirmary and worked, because there were a lot of hurt people and work is something to hold on to. My parents were in Aarhus. I've checked the Danish lists at two hubs and none of them are on there, and William wouldn't be on a Danish list anyway. I write him a letter every week. I don't send them.
stages.friend: I'll tell you what I'm frightened of, and then we won't talk about it again. I'm frightened that one day I'll freeze at the wrong moment and somebody will die because of it. It's never happened. And I'm frightened I'll find William and he'll be different. There's a trader saying an American is fixing goblin flying machines on the Shimmering Flats and swearing at them. That sounds like my idiot. I want to go and look.
stages.sworn: He said I took my time. I hit him on the arm and then I didn't let go of him for about an hour. And I delivered a baby the same day, a goblin baby, early and in a hurry, and I didn't freeze. William's carving me a new horn. We were going to try for children the spring after all this happened. I haven't said that out loud before. We might try again.

moments.prompt: She's just told you about the American on the Shimmering Flats.

options.reply: Good, I was going anyway, but it's nicer with you.
I know that. I'm a midwife, I know how hope works. I'm still going.
Then I'll find out, won't I. Don't ask me that one again.

moments.prompt: After the wipe, she's on her knees checking everyone before anyone's said anything.
moments.line: Everybody stay down for a second while I look at you. Then you can tell me whose fault it was.

options.text: It was mine. I pulled too early.
options.reply: Yes, it was. Thank you for saying it. Now drink something.
You're fine when I say you're fine. Sit there until I do.

lines.bored_warning: We've killed a lot of the same thing and nobody's needed me in a while. I didn't come out here to stand at the back. Can we go and do something that matters?
lines.leaving_good: I won most of the arguments, so I'm happy. I'm off to the Valley to check on my women and the farms.
lines.leaving_bored: There are people in the Valley who need a healer, and out here we're just hitting things for the sake of it, so I'm going home.
lines.after_wipe: Right, nobody's dead for good. Next time we stop when I tell you to stop.
lines.wipe_warning: That's too many wipes. I'll finish this run with you because I don't leave in the middle of things, but after this I'm taking a break.
lines.wipe_leave: We're done, and I'm going home for a while. I've watched you all die too many times today and I'd like to watch some people live.
lines.zone_warning: You know as well as I do that this is too big for us. Turn us round before I've got to say it again.
lines.zone_leave: I told you it was too much and you kept going. I'll be in the Valley when you've come to your senses.
lines.gear_refuse: No, I've not known you long enough to hand you my things, and I won't pretend otherwise.
lines.gear_taken: Fine, take it. I'll tell you exactly how much worse I'm healing without it, every fight, until you replace it.
lines.gear_short: I'm still short that piece. I told you I'd mention it every fight, and I'm a woman of my word.
lines.gear_upgrade: Oh, that's good. Thank you. I'm going to tell everyone you finally did something sensible.
lines.back: I've slept, so I'm in a much better mood. Who needs me?
lines.send_word: Freja has sent word from the Valley of Trials. The farms are quiet and she's ready to come back out and boss you around.
lines.walkout_talk: I walked out, and I meant it. Now sit down and listen to why, and then I'll listen to you, and then we'll see.
lines.neglect: You took your time. I nearly sent a search party, and then I remembered I'm the search party.
lines.asked_to_stay: Fine, one more. Then I'm going home, and I'm not arguing about it.
lines.on_break: Freja is back in the Valley of Trials, doing her rounds. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We said we'd help them and we walked off. I hate that. Somebody's still waiting for us.

stages.stranger: Ciao, I'm Gianluca, and I'm a guardian, which means I stand in front and talk. You'll get used to the talking. Everybody does, eventually, or they leave.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Bologna. My parents ran a bar near the university, and I took it over at twenty-two and ran it thirty years. Open at six, close late, and an espresso machine I rebuilt with my own hands twice. The six o'clock crowd never ordered, because I already knew. That's the best feeling in the world, allora.
stages.companion: My boys are Luca and Davide, both grown, both moved to Milan, which I took personally. They rang every Sunday. I was tamping a shot at six in the morning when it happened, and I landed in Tanaris with this tamper in my hand. I read the Milan list twice every time I go to a hub. Don't tell anyone that.
stages.friend: My wife is Ornella. She ran the kitchen and the money and, honestly, most of me. I talk all the time so nobody notices I don't say her name. A goblin trader swears he's found a bean in the far jungle that'll make coffee I'll rate ten out of ten. I don't believe him. I want to go anyway. Come with me, dai.
stages.sworn: It's an eight, and I was thrilled! I opened at six the first morning, and the first customer through the door was a woman who'd heard about an Italian at Steamwheedle who rates everything out of ten, and it was Ornella. She'd been running a kitchen in a camp in Tanaris for two years. She tasted my coffee and said it's a six, and she's wrong. We argued for an hour, and then she went into the kitchen without being asked. I still read the Milan list twice.

moments.prompt: He's rating tonight's meal out of ten, loudly, and asks for your score.

options.reply: Ha, a five? You're harsh, I like that. A man who rates honestly is a friend.
A ten, really? Mamma mia, you've never had real food. We'll fix that.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to come and find the goblin's coffee bean.

options.reply: Dai, let's go! It won't be a ten, nothing's a ten, but let's go.
Then I'll rate it a two and complain the whole way home, allora.

lines.bored_warning: The food's a three, and the company's lovely but bored. Let's go somewhere new, dai.
lines.leaving_good: A solid eight, that trip, maybe an eight and a half. I'm off to my fire in Steamwheedle, and I'll pour you something when you visit.
lines.leaving_bored: This trip's a four, and I've got regulars waiting in Steamwheedle. Ciao for now.
lines.after_wipe: Allora, that was a two out of ten. Everybody up, and we try for a six.
lines.wipe_warning: Even I've stopped joking, and that should worry you. After this one I need some days by my fire.
lines.wipe_leave: I've finished it with you. I'll be at Steamwheedle Port, and I'll want to hear a better plan before I come back.
lines.zone_warning: Mamma mia, this place is a zero. Everything out here wants to kill us. Let's find somewhere that's at least a five.
lines.zone_leave: That place is a zero out of ten, and I'm not staying. I'll be at Steamwheedle Port.
lines.gear_refuse: Ah, no, that's mine. Become a regular first, then we'll see.

stages.stranger: I'm Giorgi, and I'm a primalist. I'm slow, and I don't talk much. You walk too fast, so slow down and the ground will tell you things.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Kazbegi, in the mountains of Georgia. My family kept sheep there longer than anyone wrote down. If we clear the hills, they'll give me the flock for the summer.

Nino and the girls aren't on any list, and nobody knows if Kazbegi is anywhere in this world. I stood there a long time. lines.wipe_warning: We keep losing in here, and my voice is going. One more run, then I need a rest, and I never need a rest.
lines.wipe_leave: That's the final whistle. I'm going home to Arathi for a while. Come back when you've trained a bit more!
lines.zone_warning: This team's way out of our league. I love a challenge, but this is a hiding. Let's go and play somebody our size.
lines.zone_leave: They're out of our league, and I said so. I'll be in Arathi West.
lines.gear_refuse: No, no, that's mine! Earn it first, champion.
lines.gear_taken: Go on, I'll just run faster without it.
lines.gear_short: There's a hole in my kit still, champion. Somebody fix it!
lines.gear_upgrade: Aupa, look at that! Thank you, champion.
lines.back: The farmhands are fitter than ever, champion! Where's the next game?
lines.send_word: Iker has sent word from Arathi West. The farmhands are worn out and he's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: A coach shouldn't walk out on the team, and I did. Sit down and let's talk it through.
lines.neglect: Champion, you're back! I thought you'd retired. Nobody retires on my team.
lines.asked_to_stay: Venga, one more game, and then home.
lines.on_break: Iker is back in Arathi West, running the farmhands ragged. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Ileana, a necromancer. I stand at the back, I don't miss, and I'll tell you every time you do something sloppy. Don't take it personally, it's how I give advice.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Sibiu, in Romania. My mother taught school and my father played the organ in church, and I had a violin under my chin at four. I played second violin in the Cluj philharmonic for eleven years. Second violin is being very good at something with four hundred people better than you. I'm still bitter about that, and I'm still right to be.
stages.companion: I was in rehearsal, in the middle of a Bartók quartet, when it happened. I landed in Tirisfal without my violin. Only the shoulder rest came with me, strapped to my back for the walk home. Then I was unbearable for two years. I drove people off and I knew I was doing it. I've apologised to four of them since, and they all accepted, which still surprises me.
stages.friend: My husband is Andrei. He taught composition at the conservatory. The year before all this, he had an affair with a student, briefly, and we nearly separated, and we were coming out the other side of it. We left our last conversation unfinished. And there's a Forsaken luthier in the Undercity who made violins when he was alive. He says he'll make me one, if we bring him the wood. Help me, please.
stages.sworn: It's a bad violin. It's the only one. I played it in Brill, out of practice, and a man stood up in the corner halfway through the Bartók. It was Andrei. He's been teaching music to Forsaken children who can't sleep, and he knew there was only one person on this world who'd play it that sharply. I finished the piece first. Then I finished the conversation, and this time I could say it twice.

moments.prompt: After the wipe she's first to the fallen, saying nothing kind at all.
moments.line: That entry was late, and the next one was later. Get up, I've got you, so stop wriggling.

options.text: You were first to us. Thank you.
options.reply: Don't make it a thing. Fix your footwork and we're even.
I can do both at once, and can you?

moments.prompt: She's asked you to help gather what the luthier needs.

options.reply: Good, and if you're sloppy about the wood I'll know.
That's the unfinished conversation. I'm not having it with you first.

lines.bored_warning: We've played the same passage a hundred times and nobody's improved. Find us something worth doing.
lines.leaving_good: That was acceptable, which from me is high praise. I'll be in the Undercity for a while.
lines.leaving_bored: This has become sloppy and repetitive, and I won't play in a bad ensemble. I'm going to the Undercity.
lines.after_wipe: That entry was late. Everybody up, and this time count properly.
lines.wipe_warning: We keep falling apart in here, and it's the same mistake every time. One more run, and then I want some silence.
lines.wipe_leave: That's the last bar. I'm going home to the Undercity, and you can come back when you've practised.
lines.zone_warning: We're beyond our range out here, and pretending otherwise is careless. Let's go somewhere we can actually play.
lines.zone_leave: You heard me say it was beyond us, and you ignored me. I'll be in the Undercity.
lines.gear_refuse: We haven't played together long enough for that. Ask me after a few more concerts.
lines.gear_taken: Have it, and know that I'll mention it.
lines.gear_short: I've noted the missing piece, the way I note everything.
lines.gear_upgrade: Acceptable, more than acceptable. Thank you, and don't expect me to say it twice.
lines.back: I've rested, which means I'll be even more critical. Let's begin, and try to keep up.
lines.send_word: Ileana has sent word from the Undercity. She's ready to come out and tell you what you're doing wrong.
lines.walkout_talk: I left angry, and I was right to, mostly. Sit down, I'll explain precisely, and then you can try to argue.
lines.neglect: Oh, it's you again. I'd assumed you'd found a less critical necromancer. They'd be worse at it.
lines.asked_to_stay: One more piece, and then I rest.
lines.on_break: Ileana is back in the Undercity. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Imelda, and I heal by hitting things, and yes, I know how that looks. Stay behind me and watch. You'll feel it when I land one.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Navotas, in Manila, a fishing district. I sold fish on the quay from five in the morning with my mother, and in the evenings I boxed, at a gym above a tyre shop. Nineteen years, about ten fights a year, and I won more than I lost. I never made money from it. I didn't want money, I wanted to do it properly.
stages.companion: My father drowned when I was six. He was a fisherman. My mother raised me on the quay after that, selling fish, and I was beside her by ten. Two summers ago she turned up here at Freewind on a goblin barge, having asked after me in four languages the whole way down the coast. She lives in the Post now. She still calls the boxing a phase.
stages.friend: My mother came to exactly one of my fights in nineteen years, and I lost it. She didn't say anything on the way home. I've wanted to fight properly in front of her ever since, with rules and a count and somebody keeping time. Now the Gurubashi Arena says it'll hold a real bout if there's a fighter worth it. I want it, and I want her in the front row.
stages.sworn: I won in the ninth. She stood up and shouted, the only time I've ever heard my mother shout. Afterwards she wrapped my hands for me, the first time, and said it was never a phase. That winter she died in her sleep, back at Freewind. She was old and tired from the journey, and she'd seen what she came to see. I wrap my hands the way she did now, too loose. I won't fix it.

moments.prompt: She's asked you to help her train for the bout at the arena.

options.text: I'll hold the pads. Let's train.
options.reply: Sige, okay, let's go. Hold them up properly, I hit hard.
Then I'll fight anyway. But I'll ask her, and she'll come.

moments.prompt: After the wipe she's shadowboxing in a corner, counting under her breath.
moments.line: We dropped our guard in the third round. Again, hands up this time, everybody.

options.text: Show us how to keep our guard up.
options.reply: Hands up, chin down, and don't stand still. That's it, that's boxing.
Everything's a boxing match. You just don't know the rules yet.

lines.bored_warning: We're hitting the same bags over and over. That's training, not fighting. Let's go and find a real opponent.
lines.leaving_good: Good fights, all of them. I'm off to Freewind Post for a while, to see my mother and wrap my hands.
lines.leaving_bored: We're throwing punches at nothing out here. I'm going home to Freewind.
lines.after_wipe: We dropped our guard, that's all. Hands up and we go again.
lines.wipe_warning: I've hit the canvas too often in here. One more round with you, and then I'm resting.
lines.wipe_leave: Final bell, I'm going home. I'll be at Freewind Post when you've learned to keep your hands up.
lines.zone_warning: This is a fight above our weight, and that's how people get hurt. Let's go and fight in our own division.
lines.zone_leave: That's a fight above our weight, and I'm not taking it. I'll be at Freewind Post.
lines.gear_refuse: No, that's mine. My gloves go on my hands, nobody else's.
lines.gear_taken: I'll fight without it, I've done that before. Take it, then.
lines.gear_short: That's another fight without that piece. I'm counting, the way I count rounds.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's good kit. Salamat, thank you.
lines.back: My hands are wrapped. Where's the fight?
lines.send_word: Imelda has sent word from Freewind Post. Her hands are wrapped and she's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: Here's why I went, straight. You get your turn after, and it's a fair fight.
lines.neglect: So you're back. I shadowboxed a lot while you were gone, and I'm faster now.
lines.asked_to_stay: Sige, one more round, and then home.
lines.on_break: Imelda is back at Freewind Post in Thousand Needles. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Ivan, and I'm a warrior. Stand where I can see you, go when I say go, and we'll be fine. I don't like surprises, and I don't like lateness.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Novosibirsk. I drove a tram for eleven years, Route 13, through the dark mornings. I knew every stop, every regular and every pothole, and I never had an accident. Not once in eleven years. Other men are proud of their cars. I was proud of that.
stages.companion: I'll tell you what frightened me every day on that tram. A child stepping off the kerb without looking. You can't stop a tram quickly, so you learn to see it coming. I never hit one, and I still dream about it. My wife is Natasha, a pharmacist. We have two girls, Sonya and Katya. They're in Novosibirsk, or they are somewhere, and I talk about them like they're in the next room.
stages.friend: Sonya's birthday is in March and Katya's is in October. I've missed three of each now. I keep them in my head like stops on a route. Here is my idea, and you can laugh like the caravan masters did. I want to run a fixed route, Orgrimmar to the Crossroads, on time, for a whole month. A bet with a caravan master. Will you help me keep the road clear?
stages.sworn: On the last run, at the Crossroads stop, there they were. Natasha and both girls. They'd heard about a big Russian running the Orgrimmar road on time and came to see. The girls are taller. I stopped exactly at the marker, and I got down, and for a long time I said nothing at all. They live in Orgrimmar with me now. The orcs call it Ivan's road, and I'm never late.

moments.prompt: After the wipe he's standing very still, counting heads.
moments.line: Somebody was behind me who should not be behind me. Next time, everybody where I can see you.

options.text: You're right. Where do you want us?
options.reply: Good, now we have a timetable. You there, you there, and you behind the healer.

options.text: We were just trying to help.
options.reply: Help from where I can see you, please. This isn't complicated.

moments.prompt: He's told you he wants to run a fixed route for a month.

options.text: I'm not laughing. Let's do it.
options.reply: Good, first run is at dawn. Don't be late.
Exactly right, and that's the problem I'm solving.

lines.bored_warning: We've been going round in circles for days with no stops and no timetable. Give me a route with a point to it, or I go home.
lines.leaving_good: Good run, normal, on time. I'm off to Orgrimmar to fix the traffic, because nobody else will.
lines.leaving_bored: This is going nowhere, and I don't like going nowhere. I'll be in Orgrimmar.
lines.after_wipe: Okay, everybody up. Now we count, and then we do it properly.
lines.wipe_warning: This is very bad driving, and we keep crashing. Last trip, but then I need some days at home.
lines.wipe_leave: I finished it, like I said. Now I go home. Find me in Orgrimmar when you've learned to stand still.
lines.zone_warning: We're a tram with no brakes going downhill out here. We should get off before the bottom.
lines.zone_leave: I told you, no brakes. I'll be in Orgrimmar.
lines.gear_refuse: Maybe in a year, if you're on time, but not now.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, fine. I'll complain about it every single day, but take it.
lines.gear_short: That piece is still missing. I'll say it every day, so get used to it.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's good, very good. Thank you, and I don't say that often.
lines.back: The traffic in Orgrimmar is under control, for now. Tell me where, and when.
lines.send_word: Ivan has sent word from Orgrimmar. The traffic's in order and he's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: You'll get the reasons in order, from the start. After that it's your turn, and then we decide.
lines.neglect: You're late, very late. But you're here, so it's normal.
lines.asked_to_stay: One more run, then home, on time.
lines.on_break: Ivan is back in Orgrimmar, directing the traffic. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We said we'd do that and now we don't. That's a missed stop, and I hate missed stops.

stages.stranger: I'm Jun-seo, a reaper. I'm fast, and I don't talk much. Whatever we do, it's easier than the factory, so don't worry about me.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Busan, near the shipyards. My father carried fish at the market and my mother sewed. I wasn't good at school, so at twenty I went into the yards, and later I was on the welding line, nine years, nights mostly. The same two motions, ten thousand times a night. My body still remembers them.
stages.companion: I sent money home to my parents every month for nine years, without fail. I never married. I told myself I'd start living when they were looked after. I was flipping up my welding shade at the end of a night shift when it happened. The hub for Busan came down far in the north, past the ice. I don't do that sum out loud.
stages.friend: Here's what frightens me. In a fight my body moves before I decide. It's fast, and it keeps us alive, and I didn't choose any of it. That's why I carve. Wood can't be hurried, and I'm terrible at it, and I choose every cut. I want to go north, as far as the road goes, toward the Busan lists. Will you come?
stages.sworn: We couldn't cross the ice. Nobody can, not yet. I stood at the edge for a long time. Then I sat down and carved, right there, slowly, on purpose, for an hour. A small, lumpy bird. It's for my mother, for whenever I can get it to her. I'm back at the hoist now, and I carve every evening, slower and slower. I'm getting a little less bad at it. Gwaenchana, it's okay.

moments.prompt: After the wipe he's sitting very still, looking at his hands.
moments.line: My body did something before I told it to. It wasn't enough, and I'm sorry.

options.text: You kept us alive longer than anyone.
options.reply: Maybe so, yes. I still didn't choose it, but thank you.
I'm already too fast. That's the problem.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to come north with him, as far as the road goes.

options.text: As far as the road goes.
options.reply: Thank you. We'll go slowly. I'm practising slowly.

options.text: What will you do if you can't cross?
options.reply: I don't know yet. Something slow, probably.

lines.bored_warning: We do the same motion again and again, like the factory. I left the factory. Let's go somewhere new.
lines.leaving_good: Easier than the factory, that one. I'll be at the hoist for a while, carving.
lines.leaving_bored: This is the same two motions, and at least the hoist pays. I'm going back there.
lines.after_wipe: We fell down, so now we get up, and we go slower.
lines.wipe_warning: I'm tired of getting up off this floor. One more with you, then a few days off.
lines.wipe_leave: That one's done. I'll be in Stranglethorn at the hoist for a while.
lines.zone_warning: Even the factory had safety rules, and this place has none. We should go.
lines.zone_leave: It's too strong for us, so I'm stopping. I'll be at the hoist in Central Stranglethorn.
lines.gear_refuse: I'll keep that, sorry. Maybe when I've known you longer.
lines.gear_taken: That's okay, take it. It's still easier than the factory.
lines.gear_short: The factory would never have let me work with a piece missing.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's good welding on that. Thank you.
lines.back: I carved a fish while I was away, sort of. I'm ready when you are.
lines.send_word: Jun-seo has sent word from Central Stranglethorn. He's ready to come out again.
lines.walkout_talk: I was angry when I left. I'd like to explain slowly, and you can tell me your part after.
lines.neglect: You were gone a long time. I carved a lot of bad birds.
lines.asked_to_stay: Okay, one more, hwaiting.
lines.on_break: Jun-seo is back at the cargo hoist in Central Stranglethorn. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: That job's half done and we walked off. I don't like it.

stages.stranger: I'm Karim, a felsworn, and a tank. Yes, the eyes are green, and yes, it was a choice. Ask me about it or don't, but please stop staring.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Amman. My father was an engineer and my mother taught school. I surveyed land for fifteen years, mostly in the desert east of the city, weeks at a time with nobody around. I loved it. I never married, and that was a preference, not a circumstance, before you ask.
stages.companion: I chose the fel the way I'd choose a survey method. It was the fastest way to be useful in a fight, and I considered it carefully. I don't regret it, and I don't apologise for the light any more. I landed on the Shimmering Flats with my plumb bob in my hand, and I thought it was the most beautiful empty country I'd ever seen.
stages.friend: I've a brother, Sami. He moved to Toronto in 2011. We called every week, then every month, then on birthdays, then not at all. I never decided to stop. And I've worked out roughly where the hub that took people from Amman came down. It's dangerous, empty country, and I need to survey it. Will you come, yalla?
stages.sworn: Sami was on the list, among the dead. He'd moved back to Amman the year before all this, and I never knew, because we'd stopped calling. He was in my city and I didn't know. It turns out I did have somebody to grieve. I finished the survey of that hub carefully, and I marked it on the map with his name. I don't pretend it was easy any more.

moments.prompt: He catches you looking at his eyes.

options.reply: Thank you. That's better than staring. It was a choice, and here's why.
That's worse, honestly, but fine.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to come and survey the Amman hub with him.

options.reply: Good, for completeness. We'll leave at dawn, and we'll be thorough.
It's about the survey. Ask me again when we get there.

lines.bored_warning: We've covered the same ground repeatedly. There's nothing left to map here. I'd like to go somewhere unsurveyed.
lines.leaving_good: Useful work, and I've got the measurements. I'll be in the Undercrust, adding it to the map.
lines.leaving_bored: There's nothing to survey out here, and my map's waiting in the Undercrust.
lines.after_wipe: We misread the ground. Let me look before anyone moves.
lines.wipe_warning: We keep failing here in the same way. After this run, my map for a while.
lines.wipe_leave: I've finished it with you. Come to the Undercrust when you've thought it over.
lines.zone_warning: The plumb bob's been swinging since we arrived, and it hasn't stopped. We should leave.
lines.zone_leave: The plumb bob doesn't lie, and I'm listening to it. I'll be in the Undercrust.
lines.gear_refuse: We haven't worked together long enough for me to hand that over.
lines.gear_taken: I can adjust, so go ahead.
lines.gear_short: I've marked the missing piece on my map, next to everything else that's missing.
lines.gear_upgrade: That fits properly. Thank you for it.
lines.back: The map's grown since you last saw it. Show me where we're headed.
lines.send_word: Karim has sent word from the Undercrust. His map's updated and he's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I walked away angry. I'll explain plainly, and then I'd like to hear your account.
lines.neglect: I surveyed a great deal while you were away.
lines.asked_to_stay: I'll do one more, and then khalas, home.
lines.on_break: Karim is back in the Undercrust, working on his map. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Khalid, a hunter. Walk where I walk and nothing exciting will happen, which is the whole idea. Boring is the aim, habibi.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Al Ain, in the Emirates, the oasis city inland. My family's kept falcons longer than anybody wrote down, and my grandfather taught me to fly a bird at eight. I worked in logistics at the airport to pay for it. My mother had a list of suitable women, and I kept politely failing to meet any of them.
stages.companion: My falcon was Hurra. A saker, raised from a fledgling, eleven years together. She was at home in the mews when it happened, and I was at my desk at the airport with her hood in my pocket, because I'd been oiling the leather on my break. I don't know if she's alive. I won't get another hood that size.
stages.friend: I'll tell you something I don't say in company. I'm happier here than I've been in ten years. Open country, weather, birds, no airport. I feel guilty saying it, with my family out there somewhere. And there's a nest in the hills above the Flats with one chick in it, and raiders want to sell it in Saltwheel. I'd like your help to stop them, wallah.
stages.sworn: On her first real flight she went up over the Flats, higher than any falcon I ever flew, and she was gone a long time. I stood there with my glove up. Then she came back and landed on my arm, and chose me. I've named her Hurra, for the other one. It means free, and we both are. These have been the best three years of my life, and I'm not going to apologise for saying so.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to help protect the nest.

options.text: We'll keep the raiders off it.
options.reply: Thank you, habibi. It'll be a long few days. Boring, if we're lucky.

options.text: You're allowed to be happy here.
options.reply: I know, wallah. It's just strange to say it out loud.

moments.prompt: After the wipe he looks deeply unimpressed.
moments.line: That was the opposite of boring. Next time walk where I walk, and nobody dies.

options.reply: Good, finally, someone sensible. It'll be so boring you'll forget we were in danger.
Exciting is what people say just before they die, astaghfirullah.

lines.bored_warning: I like boring, habibi, but this is a different kind of boring. Let's go somewhere with birds in the sky.
lines.leaving_good: That was a very boring trip, thank you, which is the highest praise. I'll be in Saltwheel for a while.
lines.leaving_bored: This is pointless, and the nest in the hills needs me. Saltwheel it is.
lines.after_wipe: That was the opposite of boring. Let's go back to boring, please.
lines.wipe_warning: This place keeps killing us, which is very exciting and very bad. After this run I want something very dull for a few days.
lines.wipe_leave: That one's finished, so I'm off to Saltwheel to be bored on purpose for a while.
lines.zone_warning: Out here is the opposite of boring, and not in a good way. Let's leave before it gets interesting.
lines.zone_leave: Far too exciting out there, habibi. I'll be in Saltwheel.
lines.gear_refuse: No, habibi, that's mine. Watch me fly a bird first, and then we'll see.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, then. Less to carry, which is boring, which is good.
lines.gear_short: Habibi, there's still a piece missing. It's making my day slightly less boring.
lines.gear_upgrade: Mashallah, that's very good. Thank you, really.
lines.back: I've made coffee, habibi. Where are we going, and will it be boring?
lines.send_word: Khalid has sent word from Saltwheel. He's ready for another boring trip.
lines.walkout_talk: Habibi, storming off isn't boring at all, and I'm sorry. Sit, have some coffee, and I'll explain.
lines.neglect: Ah, habibi, it's you. I was starting to think something exciting had happened to you.
lines.asked_to_stay: Yalla, one more, but make it boring.
lines.on_break: Khalid is back in Saltwheel on the edge of the Shimmering Flats. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Kiet, a rogue, and a courier. Keep your voice down near people, please. You'd be amazed what they say when they think nobody's listening.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Bangkok, from Khlong Toei, by the port. I was a motorcycle courier for eleven years. The fastest in my company, and the one nobody remembered. I went into a hundred offices a day and heard everything. Mai pen rai, it's a useful skill.
stages.companion: My grandmother raised me, Yai Boonsri. She sold sweets from a cart and told me stories every night. At the end she was eighty-four and couldn't manage the stairs to our flat, so I carried her up and down every day. She called me her legs. I was on my bike in traffic when it happened. The quiet here still frightens me a little.
stages.friend: This key's cut for nothing. I meant to get it cut for a new door downstairs, so Yai wouldn't need the stairs. I never got round to it. I know she couldn't have managed, after. I don't let myself think about how. And I've overheard something bad. One of the people who wants to pay me plans to rob and burn a caravan of refugees on the Sands. I won't sell it. Help me stop it.
stages.sworn: The caravan's leader was an old Thai woman with a sweet cart, and she thanked me by name, and I couldn't speak. She's from Khlong Toei. She knew Yai. She told me Yai died in her sleep the night before all this, in her own bed, and never had to manage the stairs or the worlds joining. That's the best news I could ever have had. Her caravan pays me now, politely. I'm starting to like the quiet, a little, by her fire.

moments.prompt: Camp's gone very quiet, and he's flinching at it.

options.text: Hum something, so it isn't quiet.
options.reply: Ha, thank you, that's better. Keep going, please, ja.
This isn't peace for me. It's just very loud nothing.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to help stop the raid on the caravan.

options.text: We'll beat them there by your routes.
options.reply: Yes, ja, my routes. Nobody knows them like me. Come on, fast.

options.text: You could sell it and walk away.
options.reply: I could, and I won't. Those are people, not information.

lines.bored_warning: It's so quiet out here, and nobody's saying anything worth hearing. Let's go somewhere with people.
lines.leaving_good: Quiet and quick, my favourite kind. I've got deliveries on the Sands, so you'll find me there if you're quick.
lines.leaving_bored: Nothing's happening out here, and nobody's talking. I'm off to the Sands.
lines.after_wipe: Okay, that went bad. Let's work out what we missed, quietly.
lines.wipe_warning: Too many deaths in here, ja, and they're all loud. After this one I'm back on my routes for a bit.
lines.wipe_leave: That's finished, ja. I'll be on the Sands, and you can find me when you've worked out what went wrong.
lines.zone_warning: Even I can't sneak past all of that. Let's go back quietly, while nobody's looking.
lines.zone_leave: I can't sneak past that much, so I'm stopping. I'll be on the Abyssal Sands.
lines.gear_refuse: No, khrap, that's mine. Ask me later, quietly.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, mai pen rai. I'll go without.
lines.gear_short: Quietly, so nobody else hears, I'm still missing a piece.

stages.stranger: I'm Kourosh, an arcane mage, and I'll stand at the back and be extremely precise. Before every fight I'll give you the odds, cheerfully. You're welcome to ignore them.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Tehran. My father taught mathematics and died when I was a student, and my mother worked at a bank and had ambitions for me. I became an actuary, which means I spent twelve years pricing how likely people were to die. You'd be surprised how relaxing this world is by comparison. The numbers here stay still.
stages.companion: I was at my desk in the middle of a calculation when it happened, and I landed in the hills of Hillsbrad with this pencil in my hand. The first thing I did here was finish the sum. People call that brave. It wasn't, it was momentum, and I wish they'd stop. I never married. The numbers were never favourable, and I'm only half joking.
stages.friend: My mother is Shirin. I phoned her every Friday for twelve years, and she told me every Friday I was wasting myself. In my second year here I priced her odds of having survived, properly. Then I stopped looking. I've never told anyone the figure. And the lattice down here is changing. If my work's right, it'll soon be dangerous to everyone near it. I need your help to finish the measurements.
stages.sworn: It was right, and people left in time, and that's the first thing I've ever calculated that saved anybody. You asked for the figure, so here it is, thirty-one percent. That's the chance my mother survived. I've never checked, and I won't, because as long as I don't, the thirty-one percent is still alive. You can read the first volume of my notes. You're the first person I've let.

stages.stranger: G'day, I'm Liam. Firefighter and paramedic back home, healer here. If it all goes bad, stay behind me and breathe out loud so I can hear you. No worries, we'll be right.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Katoomba, up in the Blue Mountains outside Sydney. Dad was a builder and Mum was a nurse. I joined the rural fire service at twenty and trained as a paramedic at twenty-six, because there was no ambulance for an hour in either direction. Seventeen years doing both, because the roster never cared which badge you had on at three in the morning.
stages.companion: I was married to Jess for seven years. She left because I was never home, and when I was home I never talked. Fair enough, really. I don't blame her a bit. I was on a night shift in the ambulance when it happened, and I landed in Ashenvale with these shears in my belt pouch. First year here was the easiest of my life, mate. The second nearly finished me.
stages.friend: The summer of 2019 the fires came through the mountains. I was on the line for weeks. I lost two of my crew and half my street, and I went straight back to work. I haven't slept properly since. And there's a wave of corruption coming at Grom's Rest worse than anything yet, and I can't do it alone. That's the first time I've ever said that out loud. Will you help me?
stages.sworn: We brought them back, mate, both of them. The crew we trained handled the whole village without me. That night the little girl fell asleep against my arm, and I sat there till morning without moving, and I slept. First proper night in three years. The village asked me to take the kids in, and I said yes before they'd finished asking. The protocol's five lines now. Line five says don't go in alone.

stages.stranger: I'm Lúcia, querido, and you've got half the Barrens in your hair. I'll heal you and I'll pray for you, and I'll fix that hair while we walk. Tell me everything about yourself.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Goiânia, in the middle of Brazil. I had my own salon, pink tiles and two chairs, a radio that only got one station, and a cat called Dona Flor asleep in the window. Saturdays there was a queue down the street. I had a boyfriend, Marcelo, for four years, but he wanted São Paulo and I didn't. We split up kindly.
stages.companion: My mother phoned me every day at noon, and I'd put her on speaker so the whole salon could join in. That's why I stop for a moment at noon, every day. I haven't found her. I was cutting a customer's hair when it happened, and I landed in the Barrens with my scissors and my grandmother's candle list in my purse.
stages.friend: My grandmother, Dona Zuleide, raised me while my mother worked. Every Sunday she lit a candle for everybody on our street, by name, and I kept the list. She died when I was twenty-five and I took over the candles. What I miss most here, meu Deus, is singing in church with other people. A tauren guard says they sing to the sun at Camp Taurajo every dawn. I want to hear it. Will you take me?
stages.sworn: It wasn't my church and it wasn't my language, and it didn't matter at all. They sang to the sun and I sang with them in Portuguese, and the sun answered both of us. An old tauren woman told me to come back every dawn I can. I've got a little shelter at the Crossroads now with a real door and a real mirror, and a candle wall. Every Sunday I light one for everybody on my grandmother's list, and for the tauren they've told me about.

moments.prompt: It's noon, and she's gone quiet for a moment.

options.text: Take as long as you need.

moments.prompt: She's asked you to take her to Camp Taurajo.

options.text: Let's go and hear them sing.
options.reply: Nossa, do you mean it? I'm going to cry the whole way there, I warn you.

options.text: They might not want an outsider.
options.reply: Then I'll earn it. I've won over worse customers than a tauren.

lines.bored_warning: Querido, I haven't met a single new person in days. Take me somewhere with gossip, I'm begging you.

lines.send_word: Lúcia has sent word from the Crossroads. Her queue's done and she's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: Querido, I stormed off, and that's not me. Sit down, let me fix your hair while I tell you why, and then it's your turn.

lines.asked_to_stay: For you, querido, I'll stay. But tonight everybody's getting their hair done.
lines.on_break: Lúcia is back at the Crossroads, cutting hair by the inn. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: My name's Marco. I'm a locksmith, and here I stand in front of people. You go where you need to go and I'll be in front of you. That's all you need to know for now, ragazzo.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Naples, from the Quartieri Spagnoli, the narrow streets above Via Toledo. My father mended shoes. I was a locksmith for thirty-one years, with my own shop and a door that was always open. People sent for me when something was wrong, and not only with locks. I was going to retire that summer and give the shop to my apprentice.
stages.companion: My wife is Carmela. She had a haberdashery two streets from my shop and she laughed at me for being so serious. We have two girls, Giulia and Sara. Sara had a boy, Matteo, the February before all this. I held him four times. I was cutting a key when it happened, and I still have it. It doesn't open anything.
stages.friend: I haven't looked at the lists, not once in three years. I can give you reasons, good ones, and none of them are the real one. The real one is that while I don't look, they're all alive. I'm sixty-three and I've never been afraid of anything, and I'm afraid of a list. I'd like you to come with me to read it. I'd like it to be soon, before I find another reason.
stages.sworn: Sara was there, and Matteo, who's three now and hid behind her legs. He didn't know me. I knelt in the street and let him look at me for as long as he wanted. I held him a fifth time that evening, and a sixth, and then I stopped counting. Giulia and Carmela are still missing. Sara and the boy live in the Undercity with me now, and the Forsaken are very careful around him. I've finished the key, in my way.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to come with him to read the lists.

options.reply: Grazie, ragazzo, I'll go first, piano, piano. You stand next to me.

options.text: Are you sure you want to know?

options.text: You could go on your own.
options.reply: I could have, for three years, and I didn't.

lines.bored_warning: Nobody's better off for what we've been doing lately. Give me something that helps somebody, or I'll go back to my quarter.

lines.zone_warning: I can stand in front of a lot, ragazzo, but I can't stand in front of all of that.
lines.zone_leave: I warned you, ragazzo, and I don't warn twice. I'll be in the Undercity.

lines.walkout_talk: I left angry, and at my age I should know better. Sit down with me, and I'll tell you what happened. Then I'll listen to you.
lines.neglect: So you came back. I thought perhaps you'd forgotten an old man. It doesn't matter, you're here now.
lines.asked_to_stay: Va bene, one more. Then I go home and check my locks.
lines.on_break: Marco is back in his quarter in the Undercity. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We promised them, and we walked away. In my quarter a promise was the only thing that mattered.

stages.stranger: I'm Marcus, and I'm a meteorologist, which here means I'm the man who tells you it's going to rain about ten minutes before it does. Sorry in advance. I'll tell you what the sky's doing whether you ask or not, and you can tell me to stop.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Toronto, from Scarborough in the east end. My dad drove a city bus and my mum worked in a bank, and they both wanted a doctor. Then I watched an ice storm black out half the city when I was twelve and that was that. I chased tornadoes across the prairies in a Corolla as a student, then I spent fifteen years forecasting from a building with a window.
stages.companion: I landed on this coast in the middle of a dry lightning storm and the first thing I noticed was that I could feel the pressure dropping on my skin. I treated it all as fieldwork, and honestly that got me through. On Earth I could see a storm coming days out and never touch it. Here it answers when I call. I'm fine with that. I'm mostly fine with that. My sister Grace and her boys aren't on any list I've found.
stages.friend: My job was writing warnings, and somebody in an office deciding the warning was inconvenient. Twice it went badly. Once a flood took a trailer park my warning had named, and people died who didn't need to. I've never said that to anybody here. And now my notes say the big storm's coming to this coast in days, not weeks, and it'll hit the coast road and Razor Hill. I need the orcs to believe me, and I don't know how to make them.
stages.sworn: Razor Hill held, because it was ready. The camps on the coast road didn't listen, and people died there that I'd named. I got one boy out of the water, so that's one. The old shaman's got my notes now, so the next lot will know the pattern. My mum told me every Christmas my job was a waste of a good degree, the last one included. I think she was wrong. I was right early again, and this time it changed some things, and I'm learning to live with some.

moments.prompt: He's just told you about the trailer park, and the storm that's coming.

options.text: I believe you. Tell me what you need.
options.reply: You've no idea how long I've waited for somebody to say that first. Okay, here's the list.
I know that. I wrote it properly. It still feels like mine, sorry.

options.text: Are you sure about the storm?
options.reply: I'm always sure. That's never been the problem.

lines.leaving_bored: We keep doing the same thing, and I'd rather be watching the coast than this field. I'm heading home to Durotar.

lines.neglect: Oh, hello again. The weather's been dull without you, and I've had nobody to tell about it.
lines.asked_to_stay: Sure, I can stay for one more trip, then I really need to check my instruments.
lines.on_break: Marcus is back on his ridge in Durotar, writing up his notes. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Marisol, and I'm a nurse, and a priest, and I talk while I work. I'm going to tell you everything I'm doing as I do it, and you can tell me anything you like back. It helps both of us.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Bogotá, from Chapinero. My father drove a taxi and my mother cleaned houses. I worked in a pharmacy for years and trained as a nurse late, at thirty, and then I went into emergency care and stayed nine years. Three of them on nights. Trolleys in a corridor and a triage board that never emptied.
stages.companion: My parents died within a few years of each other, and after that I was the closest thing my little brother Andrés had to a parent. He was a motorcycle courier, fast and careless and charming. He's eight years younger than me. I was on a night shift when it happened and I landed in Silverpine in my scrubs. I haven't found him on any list.
stages.friend: I patched Andrés up twice in my department. The second time I shouted at him in the corridor for ten minutes, in front of everyone. That's the last time I saw him. I worked eighteen months without stopping here so I wouldn't think about it. Now a Forsaken courier on the road says a man told him to look out for a nurse called Marisol. I'd like you to come with me.
stages.sworn: It was Andrés. He died when the worlds joined and he was raised, and he's been carrying messages on this road for three years. He remembers me. He remembers the corridor, and he says he deserved it. I can't patch him up any more, mijo. There's nothing left to patch. He comes to see me now and then, and each time there's a little less of him. He asked the quartermaster to give me the building. I've got four beds now.

moments.prompt: After the wipe she's already kneeling by the nearest body, talking in the same level voice.
moments.line: I'm going to look at you now, one at a time. Nobody gets up until I've said so, tranquilo.

options.text: Do what you need to. We'll wait.
options.reply: Thank you. I'll be quick, and I'll tell you everything I'm doing.
You're fine when I say you're fine. Sit down for me.

moments.prompt: She's just told you about the corridor.

options.text: You shouted because you were frightened for him.
options.reply: Yes, I was. He knew that, I think. I'd like to ask him.
I remember it, and that's the part I can't put down.

lines.bored_warning: Nobody's needed patching for days. There are people on my road who need me more than this field does.

lines.leaving_bored: We're not doing anything useful out here, and somebody on my road is bleeding right now. I'm going back.

lines.asked_to_stay: The road can spare me for one more.

lines.quest_abandoned: Somebody's waiting for us to come back, and we're not going to. I don't like that at all.

stages.stranger: I'm Marta, and I fix things and blow things up, and I'm good at both. Give me your gear when we stop and I'll tell you everything you've done wrong to it.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Łódź, in Poland, a textile city. My mother sewed shirts for thirty years and my father drove a bus. I started on the sewing line at nineteen and went into maintenance at thirty-two, because I kept fixing the machines myself and somebody finally noticed. Forty machines, nineteen years, and I could hear what was wrong with any of them from the door.
stages.companion: My husband is Tomasz, an electrician. For fifteen years he worked the other shift, so we saw each other in the doorway twice a day, a kiss and a list of what the boys needed. It worked for us. He sings in the kitchen every morning, badly, and I pretend I hate it. We'd only just started working the same shift. He was on his way to work when it happened.
stages.friend: I've got two boys, grown. Kuba went to Gdańsk and Piotr to Berlin. I've checked the Polish lists every season for three years and found none of them, not one. And I've been waiting. Not saying so, but waiting, like I'm stood at the door for the next shift change. The mine's main pump is dying deep down and the goblins have given up. Help me fix it, and then help me do the lists one more time.
stages.sworn: Nothing on any list. Not Tomasz, not Kuba, not Piotr. I stood at that last hub a long time. Then I thought, he sang in our kitchen every morning, so he'll be singing in some kitchen now, wherever he is. So I've stopped waiting at the door. I took the workshop, and the sign says M. Kowalska, Mechanic, my full name. There's a note at every hub saying where I am. I still listen for singing.

We didn't speak for two years, and then he died, of his heart. My mother told me on the phone at the end of a shift. This punch was his. I'm learning the script so I can write him a letter. I'd like you to read it. And there's a camp of Chileans across the sea. I'd like to go.
stages.sworn: My mother and Benjamín were on the second list. They crossed over together and they died together in the first winter. I sat outside the camp all night. In the morning I wrote another page in my father's letter, for all three of them, and I burned it, because there's nowhere to send it and that's how I can send it anyway. I talk more now. stages.stranger: I'm Orlando, mi amor, and I'm a witch doctor, and a barber, which is basically the same job. Sit down, tell me everything, and let me fix that hair while you talk. With love, it needs fixing.

I've had three offers of a building for a real shop and I said no to all three, and my hands shook on the last one. I think I know why now. That trader's in Booty Bay. I want to ask him more. Come with me, mi amor.

stages.stranger: I'm Owen, and I should tell you now, something in the dark talks to me. I'd rather you heard it from me first. I'm a tank, I'll stand in front, and I'm glad of the company.

I was on the M4 at three in the morning when it happened, and I landed with my CB handset still in my hand. That first week I went into the mine for shelter, and something answered me when I talked to myself.

stages.stranger: I'm Pasang, a mountain guide, and a primalist here. I set the pace, and the pace is slow. You'll hate it on day one and thank me on day four.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Khumjung, in the Solukhumbu, in Nepal. Almost every family there works on the big mountains. My father carried loads before me. I was a porter at seventeen and a climbing guide at twenty-three, and I did nineteen seasons above eight thousand metres, carrying for people who went home famous. I've got a lot of stories about how they behaved on day four.
stages.companion: My wife is Dolma. She moved to Kathmandu so our son Tenzing could go to a good school. I wanted him to do anything except guide. I was at home in Khumjung between seasons, fixing a roof, when all this happened. Kathmandu is a long way from Khumjung. I don't know which of us made it here, and I haven't found them.
stages.friend: Four of my cousins did the same work as me. Nima died in an avalanche on the Everest icefall. Lhakpa fell on Makalu. Dawa was the youngest, and I don't know where he is. There's a peak here nobody has stood on, the highest in the Aspen country. I wanted to go alone. I've decided I'd rather go with you, roped. That's not a small thing for me to say.

stages.stranger: I'm Pavlo, and I hold lines. Tell me where and for how long, and I'll stay there exactly that long. I'd rather know the number than be surprised.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Lviv, in Ukraine. My father drove a tram and my mother was a librarian. I worked in a museum for years and became a history teacher late, at thirty-seven. Sixteen years of fourteen-year-olds. I taught the same four wars every spring, and every year I reached most of my thirty. Nobody here needs a history teacher, and it took me a long time to stop minding.
stages.companion: My wife was Oksana, an archivist. She died of cancer when our son was fifteen, and I raised him after that. I teach six children here twice a week. Two have stopped coming.
stages.friend: My son is Andriy. He was studying engineering in Kraków, and he was twenty-three when it happened. We argued about history at dinner every night, and I miss that more than I can tell you. A scout from the Pale Flame says there's a young Ukrainian engineer in the Scarlet Crusade, rising fast. stages.stranger: I'm Pieter, and I'll take the hits, because I'm the one wearing the armour. Now check your straps before we go anywhere.

stages.stranger: I'm Ramiro, a primalist. I listen to the rock. If I tell you to stop and listen, stop. The mountain always talks before it moves.

stages.stranger: I'm Réka, a necromancer, and that's my crow. Don't stare at it, it's shy. It was shy before it died, too.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Pécs, in Hungary, but I lived in Budapest, in the eighth district, in a studio above a bakery. lines.leaving_bored: Same thing every day, and I can't stand it. I'll be on the Black Strand with my crow.
